They are the Speakers, or their representatives, of the provincial legislatures of Canada, who are gathered here for a two day conference under the chairmanship of your own Speaker in the area council of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. I am sure that on your behalf I can extend to them, coming from the various provincial capitals, a most hearty welcome to the nation's capital and say that we wish them well. (Translation):
I should like to call the attention of the house to the presence in the Speaker's gallery of a delegation of distinguished visitors. Among them, we find the Speakers, or their representatives, of all Canadian legislatures, who are meeting at a regional convention of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.
It goes without saying that I readily act as spokesman for all hon. members to welcome our visitors and to wish them an interesting and enjoyable stay in Ottawa.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORT ON ORGANIZATION OF NATIONAL ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George asked me for a report in connection with the centennial administration. I realize his interest, he having been connected with the Canadian centenary council, as he still is. At the time I said that in time appointments would be made, and now I wish to make a report in connection with this question.
On several occasions I have made statements to the house about the preparations for honouring Canada's centennial of confederation. These reports have been in the nature of progress reports. As the house knows, the National Centennial Act provides for a national centennial administration to carry out the national government's part in the planning of Canada's first century of confederation. The centennial administration is not intended to override or duplicate any existing agencies or departments of government. It is not established to tell Canadians

Canadian Centennial
how centennial celebrations should be conducted. It was set up to co-ordinate, to stimulate and to assist in certain specific circumstances the furtherance of this historic event.
The real success of the centennial will rest not with the plans of the government of Canada or of the provinces but will depend on the vital role of each community and every citizen. Each community, in its own way, through its own organization, can contribute toward making the entire year of 1967 something to be remembered. This is a time when every Canadian can learn more about the richness of the heritage of our country and the promises of the next century.
I am glad, and 1 know all hon. members in all parts of the house appreciate, that many cities, towns, villages and municipalities have already outlined their plans for 1967. I express the hope that other communities will follow their example. I do not believe that in the centennial celebrations there is any need for a centennial colossus organization at the top. The administration, the members of which I am about to announce, must ever be conscious of the local initiatives, of the needs, feelings, ideals and aspirations of the various areas of our country.
There seems to be some misunderstanding about the relations between the national centennial administration and the Canadian centenary council. The Canadian centenary council is a non-government organization; its membership represents, I think, some 270 private, corporate and other associations, their aim being to stimulate public interest in the centennial observance and also recommend policies to be followed in the national field. The Canadian centenary council elects its own directors and hires its own employees. The Canadian centenary council has been assured of the close co-operation of the government and also of the national centennial administration. Indeed, to ensure there is the closest possible liaison, among the appointments is that of the president of this organization to the board of the national centennial administration.
Questions have been asked about the relationship of the Canadian world fair and the centennial. I believe that the world fair, and 1 think it is so intended, should be part of and not competitive with centennial observances. Although the Canadian world fair does not fall within the jurisdiction of the national centennial administration it does provide a fitting symbol of this country's maturity at the time of her birthday party. It is part [DOT]of Canada's centennial year and the govern-

ment will, of course, give careful consideration to the fullest possible co-operation between the national centennial organization and the organization of the fair.
The provinces and municipalities will have programs and projects of their own. The federal government is asking parliament for funds which may be used for making grants for local projects. These moneys would be credited to a non-lapsing fund from year to year in accordance with the provisions of the National Centennial Act. They will be made up of projects of a lasting nature. They will not exceed one third of the agreed estimate of cost, and a provincial contribution is a prerequisite to a federal grant. Such grants will not be considered if a project is already receiving federal aid under other legislation. Applications with respect to assistance and aid in this regard should be made to the national centennial administration through the media of the various provincial governments.
With regard to the federal government's program on the centennial, final decisions on some problems have not yet been taken but a number of projects are under way. One of these is the "mile of living history" in the city of Ottawa, a restoration project already undertaken here by the national capital commission. A four block stretch of Sussex drive is being restored to reveal its fine appearance of the confederation era, when it was the main commercial street in Ottawa. The commission is engaged in acquiring the property affected, and this project will help to recreate the traditional route taken by the Governor General between the parliament buildings and Government House.
A second project by the national capital commission involves Victoria island and Richmond landing located on the Ottawa river, a short distance west of this house. Hon. members will recall that the Ottawa river was once the trans-Canada highway of its day. To avoid the Chaudiere falls the voyageur would portage his canoe at Richmond landing, and at some later period the logger had his lumber slide at this point. The national capital commission is acquiring this property in order to create there a replica of that era and those early days. Industrial and commercial buildings constructed in the past century will be demolished, railway lines will be removed, the timber slide will be rebuilt and typical log buildings of the era will be reconstructed.
As a third project the government proposes to establish a Canadian historical museum which will record and portray the whole dramatic story of the settlement and development of Canada from the days of the aborigines to our own day.

The government has also agreed, subject to the approval of the necessary funds by parliament, to bear half the cost of construction of a group of memorial buildings in Charlottetown. These buildings are being erected to commemorate the pre-confederation conference held there in 1864. As the house already knows, a special silver dollar is also being struck to commemorate that conference.
Apart from the projects which directly form elements of the centennial program, several others are closely related. The national library is to be completed in time for Canada's hundredth birthday as a confederation. In addition a large redevelopment project involving 150 acres, known as the LeBreton flats in downtown Ottawa, has been undertaken by the national capital commission and will be largely completed by 1967. Work was begun last year on the partial restoration of the historic fortress of Louisburg, which in its time was one of the strongest bastions in North America and an important seat of French colonial government.
I have referred to those various parts of the program which have been approved. In addition many more cultural, historical and ceremonial projects are receiving study. Further announcements will be made from time to time.
As I mentioned previously, the government has obtained the services of John Fisher as commissioner of the national centennial administration. I say no more regarding Mr. Fisher than this, that his people have been in Canada since the late 1780's, one of his ancestors was a father of confederation, and he himself has been known in many parts of Canada through the years as "Mr. Canada".
The deputy commissioner of the centennial is Robert Choquette of Montreal, a professional writer of great competence. He has published five volumes of poetry, three novels and two plays. He is the winner of the Governor General's award, the prix Duvernay, the prix de l'Academie Frangaise and the gold medal of literature granted by the lieutenant governor of Quebec. There will be a board of directors of not more than eight.
I should mention that there is also a conference representative of all the provinces of Canada. This conference will comprise 60 representatives, 20 of whom will be appointed by the provinces and 40 by the federal government. As far as possible-and I welcome suggestions in this connection-we want this conference to be representative of all facets of Canadian life. We want the very best people possible on this conference,
Canadian Centennial
for on it depends, in co-operation with the officers and directors, the success of the celebrations.
The six directors outside the government are all distinguished in business and community activities. They are Mr. Hugh Mills, Halifax, a merchant; Mr. Paul Desmarais, president of the Provincial Transport Co., Montreal; George Metcalf, president of Lob-law Groceterias, Toronto; J. R. Murray, managing director of Hudson's Bay Co., Winnipeg; Dr. Norman MacKenzie, former president of the University of British Columbia and president of the Canadian centenary council; Mrs. Marianne Linnell, alderman of the city of Vancouver. The government representatives are two distinguished civil servants, Mr. Ernest Cote, assistant deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources, and Dr. John Hodgson, assistant secretary to the cabinet.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORT ON ORGANIZATION OF NATIONAL ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the establishment of a council to supervise the organization of the confederation's centennial celebrations. That most important statement could very well have repercussions throughout the country.
My first reaction following what the Prime Minister said just now was not only to assure him that we are in favour of that council, to which we shall give our strongest support, but to congratulate him as far as some of the appointments are concerned. In saying so, I am thinking of Mr. Fisher and Mr. Robert Choquette.
Mr. Fisher we have known for some time. We are aware of his experience and great qualities. I feel sure he will efficiently discharge his responsibilities; at least, we prefer to see him in the role just assigned to him by the Prime Minister than in the one he had until now.
With regard to Mr. Robert Choquette, he is an outstanding representative of French Canada. He has made his mark in the literary and academic world. I am convinced that he will fill this post with dignity.
In my opinion, it is essential that Canada celebrate the centennial of confederation in a dignified and adequate manner.
It is necessary to do some of the things mentioned by the Prime Minister, and without going over them in detail, I think of the reconstruction of the Louisburg fortress, for instance.
I feel also that it is essential for us to see that confederation rests on solid foun-

Canadian Centennial
dations when we celebrate its centennial. To achieve that aim, it is imperative to rethink, to remake the constitution as it was established in 1867.
The Prime Minister, and I remind him of this with all due respect, stated recently that we should not talk about separatism but only of unity throughout the country. All Canadians have heard that statement by the Prime Minister, but we should not forget that a movement in that direction does exist and we cannot ignore it. It seems to me that the Prime Minister is not enough in contact with some segments of the people.
That is why I was saying a while ago that a new appraisal of the basis of confederation is a must so that we may all together, properly and adequately, commemorate the centenary of confederation and that all Canadian citizens may be equal partners in that new confederation.

Mr. Speaker, all I wish to say is that we welcome this announcement at this time. I am sure we can all agree there is little enough time left now to make all the arrangements and plans and co-ordinate those plans in order to be ready to have a birthday party, as the Prime Minister suggests, in keeping with the importance of this occasion.
I think we in this party can, and do, give our support to the people who have been nominated to the council. We also welcome the suggestion by the Prime Minister when he invited others to propose names for the larger convention of 60. We shall give this consideration and offer some nominations, if you like, to this council. We in this party, too, hope these celebrations will do something to further the cause of the true spirit of confederation as it was outlined nearly 100 years ago.

subtopic: REPORT ON ORGANIZATION OF NATIONAL ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the people of Canada are anxious to celebrate the centennial in the most outstanding way possible. It is certainly not too soon to begin laying plans at the federal, provincial and local levels. I am sure that Canadians generally will welcome the announcement made by the Prime Minister that the centenary committee is now being set up and that the board of directors has been appointed, as well as the commissioner and deputy commissioner.
I suggest to the government that in making the appointments to the council of some 60 members, 40 of whom will be appointed by the federal government, we ought to keep in

mind the fact that a celebration of this kind, if it is to have any meaning, must secure the participation of a good cross section of the Canadian people, and that on that committee there ought to be representatives of farm organizations, co-operatives, labour organizations, universities, and groups interested in the arts and literature, in order that people in all walks of life will feel that they have had some part in preparing this program and in order that we may have the fullest participation and co-operation from people in every walk of life when the actual centenary is taking place.
I think we shall all look forward to the list of monuments which it is hoped will be constructed in order to commemorate Canada's centenary. However, I think we ought not to lose sight of the fact that there are intangible monuments which are equally important, and we might try to set for ourselves, on the federal, provincial and local basis, some objectives in terms of health programs, welfare programs and other things that would give to the Canadian people a sense of pride not only in brick and mortar but in the social accomplishments which they have been able to attain by 1967.
Above all, it seems to me that every effort must be made by all of us to see to it that in 1967 the true spirit of confederation has been fully established and that we do everything possible between now and then to bring about a better understanding and a better appreciation of the culture and the point of view of the two great races that make up confederation.
We in this party will do everything we can to support the government in putting into effect a program of this kind, to the end that when we celebrate our one hundredth birthday we shall be a country in which we are bound together by bonds of co-operation and mutual understanding.

Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to table the report I have just received from the expert committee on the habilitation of congenital anomalies associated with thalidomide. The committee was established on the recommendation of those attending the federal-provincial conference on this subject on August 17 of last year. The committee was made up of a group of experts in various professional fields most directly concerned with rehabilitation.

At its final meeting last year, which was attended by provincial representatives, proposals were made for the techniques and principles that should be employed in the rehabilitation of children with severe limb defects. The proposals have been incorporated into the committee's recommendations, which coincide to a considerable degree with action the government is already taking. For example, one of the recommendations suggests that a short course be set up to provide training for Canadian specialists involved in this rehabilitation field, and arrangements are now being made with the child amputee centre in Los Angeles to bring a group to Toronto to provide a two week course as soon as possible. As soon as the date of this is known I shall invite the provinces to send specialists to this course. The federal government will pay the costs of presenting the course, and will share with the provinces the expenses of provincial representatives.
A second proposal is that three research and training units be developed in Canada, concerned with prosthetic services and rehabilitation for severely disabled persons. The government will seek to add $200,000 annually to the funds available under the medical rehabilitation and crippled childrens' grant to implement this proposal. The services which should be developed by this means will benefit not only children with disabilities associated with thalidomide, but others with severe disabilities from other causes.
The committee also considers that the whole problem of the training of prosthetists should be reviewed, and suitable courses established in Canada. My departmental officers are now consulting with medical educators in the rehabilitation field to determine the best way of proceeding.
The report points out that the basic components of prosthetic appliances are imported into Canada, and urges that a manufacturing potential be developed in this country. I expect that our current study of this proposal will result in satisfactory arrangements to achieve this objective very shortly.
All members of the expert committee deserve the greatest commendation on the painstaking way in which they have carried out their duties. In co-operation with the provincial authorities it is our intention to implement to the fullest extent the recommendations set forth in the report, two copies of which I should now like to table.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That means that our debate is divided into a debate on foreign policy and a debate on defence policy, I would not complain about that if there were sufficient time to deal with these two important matters because, of course, they are very closely related.
Every debate on defence policy, and I suppose this applies to a debate on foreign policy as well, is essentially a debate on the ultimate fate of men and of states, of their wisdom in directing the genius of our species so that it can create more than it destroys. At the present time it has created the possibility of the destruction of our planet, as was pointed out by hon. gentlemen who spoke on this matter yesterday. Foreign policy of course, Mr. Chairman, is or should be the foundation of defence policy which is designed to support it. In our country neither foreign policy nor defence policy will be strong and purposeful unless Canada itself is strong, united and resolute, and that means above all Canadian unity on the basis on which we decided it in 1867, and a strong, independent Canada.
Canadianism, Canada first if you want to call it that, must reflect this national unity. It is, of course, as is so often said and so profoundly true, not national uniformity. Canada is composed of two races, two cultures, two languages, two traditions to which have been added those of many other people which have given colour and strength to the pattern of our national development.
But there is something else, Mr. Chairman, both in foreign policy and in defence policy. The national independence which I have mentioned, most especially in the day and age in which we live, must be qualified by the necessities of interdependence. No country, least of all a country in the position of Canada, can live unto itself alone. Canada first must never mean Canada only, nor in our time has it done so. By far, Mr. Chairman, at the moment the most important of Canada's political, material and economic relationships with any other country is that which we have with our neighbour the United States, which by its power has become the leader of the free world; a country which by its policies or even by its lack of


policies so greatly influences our own destiny as well as the destiny of every other country in the whole world. How we manage our relationships with our neighbour is one of the most important aspects, and in some respects is the most important aspect, of our foreign relations, of our foreign policy.
It is also a test of maturity and the good sense of Canadian nationalism, to say nothing of Canadian politics. We must, of course, stand up for our rights as Canadians. We must protect our national interests. We must speak and act firmly when those rights and those interests are threatened by American action or by the action of any other country. We must not, and we never have, become merely a satellite of any other state. But we would be pretty foolish if we tried to put ourselves alone in orbit. We must realize that a separate Canadian identity, a strong and independent Canada, does not and cannot mean either isolation or immunity. It is well to remember this while living in the shadow of the United States. It is also well to remember that, while living in the shadow of the United States has its problems and its worries for us, living without her free strength in a turbulent and dangerous world, living with a communist state as our land neighbour instead of the United States, would be a far more difficult and far more dangerous situation for us.
Perhaps it is just as well to remember also that the Soviet union, if not our land neighbour, is certainly our ice neighbour. So we do not prove our Canadianism, Mr. Chairman, but only our immaturity when we confuse the defence of Canada's rights with emotional breast beating or by criticizing whatever symbol of Americanism we think at any particular moment requires such criticism. There is more to our relationship than that. We worry not only about our general political and strategic relationships on this continent, but we worry, also and quite rightly, about United States control of so much of our industry and our natural resources. So we should, especially since it has increased in the last five years during a time when we were to be saved from this kind of domination.
It started under the Liberals.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps it did start under the Liberals. It started a long time back under both the Liberals and the Conservatives. I have some doubts about the ability of my hon. friends in the far corner to save us by their own magic nostrums from this kind of development.
In our worry over United States economic penetration, however, and any policies designed to check it-and we should have such

policies-we should not forget that United States capital has been responsible for much of that Canadian development of which we are so rightly proud and about which we boast.
Shame.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If that shout of 'shame' means anything, Mr. Chairman, then the hon. members who make it should take steps to keep all United States capital out of our land. I wonder what would happen to our country if that were done. I wonder particularly what would have happened to the province of Alberta if that had been done. We should also remember, Mr. Chairman, that when this capital from abroad comes into our country it is subject to our laws as well as to our criticisms.
Not always.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is subject to our laws. Canada makes the laws that cover Canada and activities in Canada. If we allow Canadian development to be controlled by the United States dollar, if we allow Canadian values and Canadian identity to be destroyed by the less attractive aspects of United States life and culture, this will be because we did not ourselves care enough about it to do anything effective. The fault, dear Brutus, may lie in us as well as in the stars and stripes. I apologize for my misquotation of Shakespeare in the presence of a Shakespearean expert in this house.
I hope that our worries about our neighbour, and they are understandable, will not obscure a far greater cause for worry and for fear, namely that in the world today the greatest danger of losing even the peace we have is not from American imperialism but remains from communist international imperialism with its dynamic and revolutionary aggressiveness, an aggressiveness which now seems to be centered in Peking, not Moscow. It is not the United States of America which causes us in this country to spend $1.5 billion a year on our defence.
An essential condition for a better world- one essential condition, and there are certainly others-is the closest friendship and the best possible relations between the United States and all the free democracies, including Canada. The first objective of those whom we have most reason to fear-although I hope that cause will diminish over the years and I acknowledge that there are some indications of progress in that regard-is the weakening and the ultimate destruction of such good relations between the United States and other free democracies. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I repeat that in foreign affairs any Canada first policy must not mean isolation 27507-3-197
Supply-External Affairs or neutralism, nor should it discourage in any way the policy of building up other associations, a British commonwealth of nations or an Atlantic community.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The ultimate ideal, of course, is not a regional one, but universal, collective security and peace through a universal organization, the United Nations. But until that ideal is realized-and we in this house made this decision a good many years ago

we must rely on regional action, particularly at present through NATO.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization today remains essential for collective action by the free states which are its members. Those who advocate its disbandment, as the New Democratic party does, along with the Warsaw pact, do no service to peace or security. If the NATO organization goes, then its members return to purely national defence and to national foreign policies, "each nation for itself and God for us all." But if, on the other hand, the Warsaw pact goes as part of the bargain, communist control exercised from Moscow will remain in exactly the same manner in terms of the reality of the control. There will, in reality, be little or no change.
If NATO, however, is to remain strong and effective-and this has been said by so many so many times in this house and outside that it is becoming a cliche, but it is a cliche which has become a cliche because it is so fundamentally true-it must be a genuine partnership with a maximum of consultation so that members can act together in an emergency, and that means consultation wherever possible before an emergency develops. A take it or leave it attitude by any one member could provoke, or where it may already exist could strengthen, a go it alone reaction by another, and that reaction would express itself not only in foreign and defence policy, especially in building up separate, independent nuclear forces, but also in inward looking and discriminating trade arrangements, either national or regional.
The Atlantic alliance will not survive without this concept of partnership being carried out in practice, and without co-operation and mutual confidence. Jealousy and petty nationalism could easily kill it. If any member of the alliance thinks more of national power or national glory, and allows the prerogatives of independence to frustrate the necessities of interdependence; if a member permits a "my country first" attitude to jeopardize that country's relation with its friends in the alliance, that could certainly destroy the alliance.

Supply-External Affairs
Mutual confidence could also be destroyed either by refusing to accept a fair share of the common defence burden, because that is what collective defence should mean, or by unilaterally rejecting pledges already accepted, commitments already accepted by refusing to take the steps necessary to carry them out. That, of course, brings me to the whole question, the other side of the coin, the question of national defence policy itself.
Mr. Chairman, as I said at the beginning this is an unusual discussion of defence policy. It is confined to these two days, and we are asked to cover the whole field of foreign affairs and defence in these two days at the end of which, because of the nature of the discussion, there will be no motion possible which could be moved in order to test the feeling of the house in respect to any particular subject of external affairs or defence. It seems to me this kind of debate on these two matters, after we have been so long prevented from debating them at all, since last September, is an evasion of responsibility for providing a more meaningful discussion of such a vital matter.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In the five years since the present government took over I doubt if there is any parliament or legislative assembly in the democratic world which has had less discussion of, or less information submitted to it on, defence policy than has this parliament and the previous parliament. If you compare the discussions in congress, in Westminster and in Paris you will know what I mean.
We have had no adequate statements in recent months by government spokesmen on defence policy. Perhaps the reason for that may be differences of opinion inside the government. A house divided is not likely to welcome people to come inside. We have had no committee of the house set up on defence policy, although the request for such a committee has been made in this house more than once. We have had no realistic and responsibile statements from the government, especially since this parliament met, on this most vital of all matters, vital because it concerns peace and war. We on this side have pleaded for a defence policy committee to be set up, and other opposition parties have joined in that request.
I know, as the Prime Minister has already pointed out, that normally after a government has made up its mind on these matters, parliament agrees on them by parliamentary discussion. But in the circumstances of today and because of the situation in which we now find ourselves in view of what has happened

during the last five years, things are not normal; and certainly it would be desirable, even now, to set up a small committee on defence policy which could call witnesses, get information and discuss this question, so that we could see how much agreement we could reach on it.
That has not been done. It presumably is not going to be done as long as the present government is in power. But at least as a substitute for a defence policy committee we might have had from the Minister of National Defence, before this discussion took place, some kind of white paper on defence which would put forward the policy of the government in these matters. Not only have we not had that, but so far in this debate we have not had a single statement from any member of the government side on defence, not a word. It remains for the three opposition parties to declare their position and their views on defence policy in the absence of any statement from the Prime Minister or any member of the government on that policy. This to say the least, Mr. Chairman, is a reversal of the usual and accepted democratic parliamentary practice.
Any opposition, of course, is at a disadvantage in discussing defence matters because only the government has all the information which can be used as the basis for defence policy. Although a lot of that information cannot be made public in parliament, surely the government has an obligation to make a statement based on the information which it has, and some of which it should make public before there is a debate in the House of Commons on defence policy. Surely it was essential for some government spokesman to have made a full and frank statement on defence policy yesterday. Perhaps they will do so today, Mr. Chairman.
We all know that the only sure and enduring basis for defence, that aspect of defence policy which makes most sense, is ways and means of keeping the peace. We all know now that no country, however powerful, and no agglomeration of countries, however powerful, can win an all-out nuclear war. Indeed, we are told by experts that it is impossible to even wage one. This makes it more necessary than ever to prevent one.
As part of this process in the world in which we live we have to have a defensive force, a deterrent force if you like, including a nuclear deterrent force. This deterrent force is required to preserve the peace until we reach a state of affairs where the foundation of peace will be stronger even than that of force. I pay tribute to the sincerity and the work of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his efforts, with others, to try to

find that kind of foundation. I accept that position, as I am sure do most hon. members, if not all, in this house. The only sincere alternative to the acceptance of this position is one of neutralism or pacifism. These can be very honest alternatives, though I believe they are misguided, unwise and dangerous, and I can see no safety in them.
Today, then, defence policy is based, as I have already indicated, more on the interdependence than the independence of nations. We know that no country can defend itself alone. We know that the only security, especially for a country like Canada, lies in collective action through a defensive alliance such as NATO, which rests, or should rest, so far as its military side is concerned, on a pooling of strength to which every member of the alliance makes its contribution. Collective defence of this kind is based on treaties, on arrangements, on pledges, on obligations undertaken, on commitments given among the member states, as well as commitments and pledges made by the member states to their own people.
When dealing with our friends inside an alliance we assume that pledges made will be kept, that commitments undertaken will be carried out. We also assume that a change of government will not necessarily mean a sudden and unilateral renunciation of defence obligations or military pledges which have been made. If we assume that, our friends have the same right to assume that the pledges of the Canadian government are the pledges of the nation; that they will not automatically disappear with a change of government; that they will be changed only by agreement, when they affect other members of the coalition; and that until changes are made by agreement, they will be honoured.
To find the best defence policy for Canada- and I cheerfully admit this-would be a difficult enough problem in any circumstances and for any government. But it has been confused and indeed complicated by the controversy over one aspect of this policy. It has been confused and complicated by other things, but I am now going to refer to only one subject of confusion and complication. That is, whether to use or not to use nuclear weapons of any kind and, if they are to be used, whether they should be under national, joint, or collective control; and, indeed, who should have the custody of them inside a coalition.
As was pointed out by my hon. friend from Red Deer last evening, the use of these weapons-and this has been pointed out by others also-has been made into a moral question. That, of course, makes explanation difficult because it arouses strong emotions, 27507-3-1974
Supply-External Affairs understandable strong emotions, which are concerned not only with human behaviour but with the very survival of mankind, because of what these particular weapons can do. Whether Canada in present circumstances uses defensive tactical nuclear weapons or not-and they are the only ones in question; no one suggests for a minute that we should take part in the strategic retaliatory nuclear deterrent in an active way-this question cannot, in my view, be decided on moral grounds without hypocrisy on our part unless we follow through on that decision with other decisions which logically flow from it. As a member of the NATO coalition we accept the nuclear deterrent in the hands of the United States as essential for defence, and we supply much of the uranium which goes into United States nuclear bombs. Therefore to say that on moral grounds we shall not accept any nuclear weapons in any circumstances is dishonest and hypocritical unless at the same time we are willing to withdraw from NATO or refuse to export to anyone uranium for military defence purposes.
The fact is, of course, that the argument for or against nuclear weapons for Canada is a political and military one, not a moral one. In saying that I am not ignoring the fact that there are moral considerations involved and that this weapon does not involve for many people a moral problem. It certainly does, but the moral problem, in my view, is concerned not with the weapon itself but with the use of the weapon; certainly not with the kind of weapon we are discussing at this time as part of the defence policy of Canada. The moral problem is concerned not so much with the weapon as with war itself, which is the basic and ultimate immorality.
As I see it, the question we have to ask ourselves is, how can Canada make her most effective military contribution to the preservation of peace and the prevention of war in co-operation with her allies-because I believe in the alliance-and how can we ensure that commitments once undertaken, pledges once given for this purpose by us in agreement with our allies can effectively be carried out until they are changed.
In dealing with this aspect of defence, the military aspect, I am aware that I am dealing with only one phase of this question. Perhaps 50 years ago if we had talked about defence in this house or in any other place we would have been talking only of the military aspect. That was defence. But there are certainly other aspects of defence now, as I mentioned a few moments ago. There is the political and diplomatic aspect; and when the Secretary of State for External

Supply-*External Affairs Affairs works for disarmament he works for defence. His work and the work of other Canadians at the United Nations over the years to further the cause of disarmament and to remove tension and fear between peoples is defence work.
There is also the economic aspect of defence. Trade, as often in the past and now, can cause conflict which could lead to trouble; therefore the economic aspect of defence consists of doing what we can in the countries of the world and especially in our own country to remove obstructions to international trade; and, what is perhaps of even more importance, providing economic assistance to materially underdeveloped countries. Because, as was pointed out by the hon. member for BurnaLy-Coquitlam last night, we may find that if we cannot make some progress on that front, then nuclear bombs, Bomarcs, air bases and all the rest will not amount to very much in the light of even more explosive problems of ignorance, overpopulation, fear, hunger and unsatisfied legitimate desires among the emerging hundreds of millions in Asia and Africa. So economics is an aspect of defence.
There is also the ideological aspect of defence, how we can strengthen the forces of freedom and the values and ideals which should flow from freedom. I suggest that in this other aspect of defence we must try in a non-military way to remove the tensions which bring fear, conflict and war and which divide us in this small world from those we fear.
All these things, of course, do not form the major subject of discussion in this particular debate, because we shall not have time to go into these other aspects of defence. Therefore I ask, on the military defence side, what is the situation in Canada especially as it concerns nuclear weapons? Well, we know a good deal more about this now than we did, say, a year ago, not because of statements made in the House of Commons but because of information which we have been able to secure outside the House of Commons and by reading the proceedings of the subcommittees of congressional committees on defence in Washington and by reading blue books which emerge from the United Kingdom House of Commons; also, of course, by some of the things which have been said in this house and outside in Canada.
In 1959 the Canadian government-I do not think this will be disputed, but I could produce lots of evidence to support this contention if it were-agreed that the role of our overseas air division in NATO, a role which from a military point of view is undoubtedly our most important contribution

to NATO, should be changed to the very important one of strike reconnaissance from high level interception. The Liberal opposition in parliament at that time, back in 1959, opposed this new and changed commitment for that air division, and we gave in some detail the reasons why we thought this was the wrong kind of role to be undertaken and why we thought it should not be accepted or, if accepted, why it should be changed before it became too difficult to change it. Nevertheless that role was undertaken, and after four years-I remind hon. members of the New Democratic party of this-after four years, because it takes that long, the equipment to discharge the role is now being delivered. I think the first planes were delivered last October for the first squadron which is to be converted to undertake the new role. The aircraft for this purpose are American Star-fighters, now CF-104's in the R.C.A.F. We are informed that one R.C.A.F. squadron will be in a position to go on alert by the end of April and the others in the weeks following. So the whole division will, at the present rate of progress, be equipped within a few months.
Now, in order to accomplish effectively the role which this division has undertaken, these planes are designed-and this was understood when the order was placed-to be armed with rockets which would have nuclear warheads. We know they cannot operate effectively to do the job which has been entrusted to them without such warheads. The government, however, having committed the taxpayers to the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars on these planes-the figure which has been given is half a billion dollars-has not made up its mind even yet whether to accept the warheads or not.
It has not even made the political agreement with the United States which is essential before the nuclear warheads could be made available if it were decided later to accept and use them. That agreement will certainly take some time to negotiate, as will the training of our airmen in the use of the weapons. According to the former NATO commander it will take from three months to six months. However, nothing has been done one way or the other. No decision has been made. I say that this has now become an intolerable situation, and that the result is now a serious gap in the defence arrangements of the NATO alliance. We said that we would assume a particular responsibility in that defence. In fact we are not doing so and no one else in the coalition can now do so, because we said we would do the job and we are supposed to be taking it on.

Similarly our NATO ground forces are being equipped, if they have not already been completely equipped, with United States Honest John artillery rockets designed to carry nuclear warheads, but the government has taken no decision to secure the warheads even though our ground forces are expected to use them for defence against attack, and everybody knows that fact. At home there are the United States Bomarc missiles, ground to air, which are in the same state of impotence or, if you like, suspended animation. I may say they certainly created a good deal of political animation. The government must have decided back in 1959 that the two Bomarc bases on Canadian soil were important links in the continental defence chain. Again we Liberals at the time thought they were wrong in this matter. We opposed the decision, but it was made by the government for Canada; and the missiles have now been delivered at the expense of the U.S.A. Whatever may be their value a year or so from now, we know they are completely useless now without nuclear warheads. We know that these warheads cannot be secured at once and used at once in an emergency. Plans must be made in advance and agreements must be reached with the United States in advance.
Our Bomarc missiles, for instance, stood inert and useless in the alert during the Cuban crisis. They might as well have not been there. That crisis also showed how absurd it is to think that a decision could be made and quick, effective action taken after the emergency developed. Yet we were told not long ago that this could be done. Similarly our CF-101 aircraft, again a U.S. plane, the Voodoo, to be completely effective as interceptor fighters even for the diminishing continental defence role which they have been asked to perform but which the military experts say is still of some importance, are designed to use nuclear weapons in the interception of attackers. It is also ridiculous to think that we can reserve the decision to get them, and have them ready for use, until after the emergency develops.
In short, both in NATO and in continental defence the Canadian government has made certain defence pledges and has accepted certain defence commitments on behalf of Canada which can only be carried out by Canadian forces if nuclear warheads are used. The government and nobody else made these commitments. Since then, however, the government has refused to make the decision either to alter the commitments or to accept the means to carry them out. Alteration, of course, is not so simple and so easy as it would have been a year or two ago. It takes years, as I have just indicated
Supply-External Affairs in connection with the air division, to implement major changes in defence policy and commitments. I say that it is humiliating and dishonourable for Canada to make pledges and accept commitments and then refuse to discharge them or put our men in a position to discharge them if they were called upon to do so in an emergency. Canada cannot maintain a position of respect and influence in the world on any such basis.
What then should the government do? It should act in order to ensure that the commitments accepted by Canada with her allies will be discharged by Canada as long as they exist. We have taken our place in a sector of the defence line. Canadians have done that previously in our history. We must be prepared to do the job in that sector until we agree to do something else. As a lady delegate, according to the press, reported to the recent Conservative convention, and I think her words bear repeating, the situation is this. I may say that this was not during one of the breakfast meetings nor indeed during one of the barbershop quartet meetings. This was at the meeting which discussed defence and nuclear warheads. This lady delegate is reported to have put the matter in this way, "We have contracted. We have this by agreement. We promised. We have no choice now whatsoever".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will get to that, too. Up to a year or so ago the government had some room for manoeuvring in this matter. Until the equipment had been delivered we could have changed the commitment without the difficulty or delay that is now inevitable. We on this side of the house thought that change should have been made to a better role, and we said so inside and outside the house. But now the rockets are with the batteries, but without ammunition. The planes are with the squadrons, but without the armament which they are supposed to have. Hence it is more difficult to make changes, and it will take longer. Meanwhile do we do nothing in respect of the commitments undertaken, as I understand would be the position of my hon. friends of the New Democratic party?
The Minister of National Defence in the House of Commons on March 20, 1962 as found at page 2012 of Hansard, stated as follows:
As the 104's have only begun to come off the production line and we are just setting up training facilities to train the crews to operate them, they will not be going into operation for a year and, as I said several times before, the matter of securing armaments for them is not an urgent matter at this time.

Supply-External Affairs
It is an urgent matter now because the planes are there and the crews are with them, and if they are to be trained they should begin to be trained now with the equipment necessary for them to do the job they were asked to do. Policy now has been translated into arms, into equipment and into organization. Surely it is idle to argue, Mr. Chairman, that you can go on shilly-shallying on this matter, that we need do nothing now because changes are taking place all over the place in defence strategy and in defence tactics. Of course they are, and they will continue to take place. That is only an argument for not doing anything at any time.
The cancellation of the Skybolt by the U.S.A. for the United Kingdom, for instance, has nothing whatever to do with this Canadian problem. The British ordered this nuclear missile from the United States. The United States stopped production of the Skybolt, which was to take the place of the Blue Streak. Then the United States offered the British, in place of the Skybolt which had taken the place of the Blue Streak, another American nuclear missile, the Polaris. To make that a situation which is the same as that with which we are faced, when we have taken on a certain job which can only be done by one particular missile at this time, when the government refuses to change the job or take the missile or get a substitute for it-surely to relate this problem to that which the United Kingdom government has and to which the Prime Minister has referred does not make any sense at all.
There is no parallel here, no excuse for inaction any more than there is in the Nassau communique which refers to discussions about a NATO nuclear deterrent force. The Prime Minister has said that this is something new, this is a new situation, this is a change, this is an important development, and we must hold back and see how it works itself out. Mr. Chairman, these discussions with regard to a NATO nuclear deterrent were first referred to in the House of Commons by spokesmen of the government back in the autumn of 1957 or the beginning of 1958, because it was at the NATO council meeting in Paris in the autumn of 1957 that the decision was taken regarding nuclear weapons for NATO even if that decision has not yet been fully implemented. Discussions have been going on for years and they will probably go on for many, many months before the NATO council and the NATO governments are able to work out a satisfactory collective nuclear deterrent; to use this as an excuse for inaction in carrying out now the pledges we have under-

taken with respect to making equipment available to do that does not, I repeat, make any sense.
It was because of the changing and shifting situation respecting nuclear equipment that we on this side four years ago opposed the taking on of commitments that required this kind of equipment which could only come from the United States. But the government brushed aside our objections and our doubts. So now let them carry through, or propose some other course which would be an effective one for Canada and agree on it with our allies. Meanwhile let us keep our pledged word.
The government, I repeat, should end at once its evasion of responsibility by discharging the commitments it has accepted for Canada and, as it happens, it can only do this now by accepting nuclear warheads for certain defensive tactical weapons, which cannot effectively be used without those warheads. An agreement with the United States for this purpose would have to be negotiated, presumably one similar to those signed by the United States government with the United Kingdom and other NATO countries to provide for joint control of the use of the weapons, if and when they are accepted. As I have said before, in such an agreement it is true that a United States finger would be on the trigger but a Canadian finger would be on the safety catch, and when we get a genuine NATO nuclear deterrent there will be other fingers as well on each safety catch.
The government position remains, however, that no decision need be made, that no action need be taken, a position which, of course, one might expect from this government. We can wait to see how the disarmament discussions get along or until an emergency develops or until something else happens. That is merely getting the worst of both worlds.
There are those who argue-I have no doubt we will hear this argument from the government side; we have already heard it from some members of the New Democratic party, and it has been referred to by the leader of the Social Credit party-that we have no nuclear commitments, that we have made no pledges to ourselves in Canada or to our allies which require the use of any kind of nuclear warhead. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is the crux of the whole question. Therefore I should put on the record the evidence which justifies the stand we have taken on this matter. The evidence surely shows how wrong that attitude is, and of this there is no shadow of doubt, no possible, probable shadow of doubt.

Let us look at the commitment or pledge. Let us go back to February 20, 1959, nearly four years ago. As found on page 1223 of Hansard the Prime Minister said this then in talking about these new weapons:
The full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads.
This is back in 1959.
The government is, therefore, examining with the United States government questions connected with the acquisition of nuclear warheads for Bomarc and other defensive weapons for use by the Canadian forces in Canada and the storage of warheads in Canada.
That was February 20, 1959.
That is not a commitment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
On March 10, 1959, as found on page 1775 of Hansard, this appears:
The government does not anticipate concluding a formal agreement with the United States government on the acquisition of nuclear warheads in the immediate future.
Naturally he was asked why, and he answered the question by saying:
-it would be some time before nuclear weapons would and indeed could be made available for use by Canadian forces.
In other words, when the weapons were made available or could be made available to Canadian forces, an agreement would then be concluded.
No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, if language has any meaning that is the only interpretation you can give it.
Case dismissed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will prove that is correct by quoting the then minister of national defence, General Pearkes, who followed this up on July 2, 1959, by saying, as found on page 5393 of Hansard:
-it is government policy that Canadian troops should be armed as efficiently and as effectively as are troops with which they are co-operating.
Then he added that negotiations were going on with the United States to make this possible. These were the negotiations that the Prime Minister talked about to make possible the acquisition of nuclear warheads for this equipment. Then General Pearkes, the minister of national defence at that time, went on to say:
-in order to arrange the details of the storing of and equipping our forces with nuclear weapons as and when they would be available and as and when we would have the weapons to launch them.
That was the purpose of the negotiations. On July 3, the very next day, the then minister of national defence said that these
Supply-External Affairs negotiations, and I quote from pages 5414 and 5415 of Hansard, "are fast reaching a stage when there can be an exchange of notes on this matter". This was in July, 1959. What were the Canadian people entitled to draw from that kind of statement by the minister of national defence?
A very weak statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It certainly was a weak statement, as it turned out, because that was four years ago and nothing has been done about it. In the same statement the minister said in the house:
I presume that eventually the Canadian forces will be equipped with atomic weapons.
Well, when is eventually? Obviously, Mr. Chairman, at the latest it should have been when the equipment, the 'planes and missiles were delivered and the commitment had by that delivery become effective. This has now happened. Later, in confirmation of this point of view, on July 22, 1959 the defence minister in an interview over the C.B.C. admitted this. He is talking now about the air division in France:
The problem will arise when our squadrons are re-equipped with the F-104G's and then armed with nuclear weapons.
I do not need to quote the position of the present Minister of National Defence on this matter because it is well known, and within the limits of cabinet propriety it has been quite consistent. All this, from the highest sources of the Canadian government, confirms what the Canadian and NATO military chiefs have known and have said; that there was indeed a nuclear commitment, both to the people of Canada and to our allies. Our allies certainly understood this to be the case. This was confirmed only Monday last by the minister of defence in answer to a question which appears at page 2920 of Hansard for that date. I will read the question: "When the government selected the Bomarc, the CF-104, the Honest John rocket and the CF-101B, was it aware that-" was the Canadian government aware- "maximum efficiency of these weapons depended on the use of nuclear armament"? The answer was, and I am sure these words were very carefully chosen:
The government was aware that in each instance these weapon systems would reach their maximum effectiveness when armed with nuclear warheads or weapons.
Surely our government does not wish to equip our troops with weapons which cannot reach their maximum effectiveness. Then the other question was, prior to acquiring these weapons did the government indicate to the United States or to NORAD or to its
3120	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs NATO allies or to NATO headquarters that it was or that it might be unwilling to accept nuclear arms? The answer was a short and categorical one, very much to the point. The answer was "No".
So much for the pledges made, the statements made and the commitments undertaken by the government, in statements in this house and outside this house. What are the commitments as understood by our allies? Last night the leader of the Social Credit group in this house said he did not know, and it was very difficult for him to make up his mind until he knew what the commitments were. I hope by now he is a little clearer in his mind in so far as statements made in parliament to the Canadian people are concerned. Let us look at the other side of the question. Was it understood by our allies that we were taking on this job?
There is no one, Mr. Chairman, who has a better right, a more respected right to speak about the North Atlantic Treaty Organization on the military side, the strategic side, than the former commander of that alliance, General Norstad. He was the commander of the NATO forces in Europe and, as I said last night, as such he was not the servant of any one government, he was the servant of all the member governments of NATO. He conducted himself properly as such while he held that command. Tribute has been paid to him by the member governments for doing so. He was not only a United States military man, he was a NATO military man, a NATO statesman and a NATO diplomat. He was the representative of all the government members of NATO. It does not seem to me to add anything to the dignity of this discussion when he is referred to, as he was by the new president of the national Conservative association, as merely a retired American general; or, according to one report when he came to Ottawa the other day, as merely an American tourist whose views are not any more important than those of any other American tourist.
Are you trying to get him on the active list again?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is very easy for my hon. friends opposite to depreciate a man whose views they accepted when he was the commander of NATO. There was not one word of criticism ever directed at him when he had this position, but when he came to Canada on a farewell visit and incidentally gave his views as a servant of Canada and when, unfortunately, he was not received by the Prime Minister but made a voluntary statement at a press conference arranged for


him at which the Associate Minister of National Defence was present, when he answered questions honestly and frankly about what we had in the way of a military commitment to NATO, when those answers did not seem to fit in with the views, prejudices, policies or desires of hon. members opposite or hon. members of the other two opposition parties, then they proceed to denigrate him, try to tear him down.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the luncheon recess I was discussing the nature of the pledges we have made on this question of nuclear weapons, the evidence to support the fact that we have undertaken certain commitments, and I had reached the point where I wished to produce some evidence, not from statements of members of the government in this house but evidence from persons outside the house concerned with the military policy of the alliance, persons who would have no axe to grind in this matter and who would presumably have the expert knowledge on which to base their information.
As I have said, this question of commitments is the crux of the situation, and I am sure the government will appreciate that because the Prime Minister has already reminded us in the house that we have made certain commitments, for instance the sale of wheat to communist China, and that we are the kind of people who honour our commitments.
At the press conference with General Norstad there was in attendance, as I mentioned this morning, the Associate Minister of National Defence, and if any of the information given by the general, who was retiring from his position as NATO commander, was inaccurate in any respect there was an opportunity for the Associate Minister of National Defence to correct the record and make sure no wrong impressions had been created. As a matter of fact I believe the general at one stage of the press conference did refer to the fact that this was a question that should be answered by a government representative.
I have before me a verbatim record of that press conference. There was nothing General Norstad said at that time that was new. It was merely confirming what had been said in the House of Commons by the opposition and by Canadian military chiefs outside the House

of Commons, but it was impressive in its confirmation of these earlier statements. At one point in the press conference, talking about Canada's commitments which was the question that had been addressed to him, the former NATO commander said this:
Canada has met those commitments in numbers and in general in quality during the entire life of the alliance.
I think that is true, except perhaps one could question whether we had met our full commitment on land, which I believe is a brigade group in Europe, and that the other components of a division in Canada be equipped and ready to join that brigade group in Europe as a Canadian division. But apart from that possible difficulty the general said we have met our commitments in numbers and, in general, in quality during the entire life of the alliance. Canada had been really outstanding in meeting its military commitments in that sense. Then the question was asked:
Q. General, do you consider that Canada has committed itself to provide its Starfighter squadrons in Europe with tactical nuclear weapons?
A. My answer to that is yes.
That is categorical and unequivocal enough. The general went on in replying to another question to say:
We established a NATO requirement for a certain number of strike squadrons. This includes tactical atomic strike squadrons and Canada committed some of its force to meet this NATO established requirement. And this we depend on.
Incidentally General Norstad added, "Again, we depend on it particularly because of the quality of that air division". Then another question was:
Does it mean, sir, that if Canada does not accept nuclear weapons for these aeroplanes that she is not actually fulfilling her NATO commitments?
The answer was:
I believe that's right. She would be meeting it in force but not under the terms of the requirements that have been established by NATO.
Then another question was asked:
General, did you say that you believe that Canada has committed this Starfighter group to tactical weapons? A. No doubt-I know that they have committed the Starfighters, yes.
Then in reply to a question dealing with the political arrangements which would be required in order to make possible political agreement with the United States in order to make it possible for Canadian forces to accept or use these weapons, and to the possibility of this resulting in a proliferation of nuclear weapons, the general had this to say:
There is no proliferation so far as control is concerned, because these weapons are held in the hands of the country of their source until they are actually used. But they can be made available fust as fast to a French squadron, to a Belgian 27507-3-198
Supply-External Affairs squadron, to a Dutch squadron, to a German squadron, to a British squadron or to a Canadian squadron, as they could be to an American squadron.
The questioner interjected:
Yes, but subject to bilateral agreement...
And the general replied:
Yes, this is subject to bilateral agreement.
Q. Would the crews be trained to use the atomic weapons?
A. Under the bilateral agreement, yes. It does take a bilateral agreement because under the American atomic energy law, if there is a bilateral agreement between two countries concerned then the information can be made available which will permit the training with these weapons and this is being done with almost all the countries of the alliance at the present time.
Then there was this question:
Q. Lacking a bilateral agreement, how long does it take to train crews?
A. You can't train them without a bilateral agreement.
Q. What I mean is, after you get such an agreement, how long would it take?
The general said:
-I think it's about six months, isn't it; three to six months minimum?
Then Air Marshal Miller, who was there, said:
Yes, but it could be done under six months.
Then General Norstad said:
It takes some time; it takes a considerable period of time.
He went on to explain, in answer to another question, that the Canadian crews have not had this training before because in earlier days the 'planes were not available, but that now the 'planes were available and they were there. Then the question was asked: With how many countries, sir, does the U.S. have such bilateral agreements for nuclear weapons?
General Norstad said:
Essentially all the countries. I can't give you the exact number; essentially all of them.
Then the question was asked:
Could you say, that the forces of what countries are actually in a position to acquire nuclear weapons immediately now in the NATO force?
General Norstad answered:
Almost all of them.
Then the question was asked:
But where are the weapons physically, are the-
Then he said this:
This is a question I cannot answer.
The question went on:
Does this mean that the Canadian forces are the only ones in the alliance that-
General Norstad broke in:
No, not the only ones. This has really not been a problem with the Canadians in the alliance up to this time. And will not become a problem until the equipment is changed.

Supply-External Affairs
Well, Mr. Chairman, the equipment has been changed and airplanes have been delivered. Then questioner went on:
Or until a bilateral agreement is signed?
A. Yes. But a bilateral agreement becomes important when the new equipment comes into the air division.
Then he added this:
I advocate the signing of the bilateral agreement because this is the only way in which you can be fully trained.
Q. When do you believe the lack of a bilateral agreement would become a problem of creating a weakness to NATO?
"A problem of creating a weakness to NATO"-and if any man was qualified to discuss the strength and weaknesses of NATO, it was General Norstad. His answer was this:
I think that it is desirable to take whatever action is necessary now, bilateral or anything else, so that the ground and air forces of Canada, which are deployed in Europe, could be used promptly with full effectiveness and I think this is important now.
Then once again the general tried to get the questioners off this question of nuclear weapons. There were questions on other subjects, but I would just like to put on the record of Hansard what the general said in winding up this press conference. He was talking about a NATO nuclear deterrent and how control would be exercised if such a deterrent force was created. He thought it should be brought under the authority of the alliance and he said:
I personally favour the authority being the authority of the alliance to the largest possible extent, and that those weapons which are developed, designed and deployed for the purpose of defending Europe, should be really controlled by the authorities, political and military, who are charged with that particular responsibility. I would like to see this within the NATO concept because I think this reduces the danger of proliferation. I think this would be satisfactory to the largest number of countries.
Mr. Chairman, I think that puts on the record the evidence given in this house which supports the view that a pledge was made to the Canadian people, and the evidence given outside this house which supports the view that the pledge was understood to be such by those who were responsible for the military side of the North Atlantic treaty alliance. Now may I, before putting forward in conclusion our own policies on defence generally, including this matter-and I can do that, I hope, very briefly-refer to what I believe to be the policy of the other two opposition parties in this matter.
The policy of the New Democratic party, as it was expressed last evening by the leader of that party, is "no nuclear weapons of any kind, in any circumstances, under any

form of control, for Canada". I think that is a fair statement of the case. Well, Mr. Chairman, that is clear not only from the statement made last evening but also, of course, from the resolutions adopted by the founding convention of that party from July 31 to August 4, 1961, because those resolutions included the following:
The New Democratic party believes that we should seek a reappraisal and change of NATO's policies and objectives.
I do not think anyone can quarrel with that. Then there was this resolution:
The New Democratic party believes that the extension of nuclear weapons to any further states and alliances threatens disaster to the world. It therefore opposes Canada's troops being supplied with such weapons at home or abroad. At present,-
I underline these words:
*-except for those nations which have independently developed atomic capacity neither NATO itself nor its members individually possess or control nuclear warheads. Should they do so, Canada must make it clear that it cannot remain in the alliance.
Those words mean, if they mean anything at all, that if there is a NATO nuclear deterrent, where the authority and control of the nuclear deterrent force would be taken out of the hands of an individual member of the alliance and put under the authority of NATO itself through a mechanism devised by the NATO council-that is, a genuine collective deterrent with nuclear defensive, tactical weapons-the New Democratic party advocate that we withdraw from the NATO alliance. Well, Mr. Chairman, we on this side of the house do not accept that position. I say with great sincerity that, while I appreciate the sincerity of hon. members of the other party who support this view, I do not believe that such a withdrawal by Canada from the alliance, in the circumstances of there being a collective nuclear, tactical deterrent under NATO, would add anything to peace or security in the world. I think it would weaken peace and security in the world. Then the resolution goes on:
To relieve tensions, Canada should press for a demilitarized zone in central Europe and-
Listen to this. I mentioned this earlier in my speech:
-for the simultaneous disbandment of the Warsaw and NATO pacts.
That puts the two pacts, presumably, on the same level of interest and importance in so far as the preservation of peace and security is concerned, and suggests that if we withdrew from both of them the balance would be maintained. I do not agree with that, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps I should add that one New Democratic party spokesman, the hon. member for York South, in explaining the policy of his party the other evening

in Toronto, and incidentally in confirming the view that the Tory government did in fact take on a nuclear commitment as far back as 1959, made a statement about Liberal party policy which is completely false when he said on January 5 as reported in the press:
The agreement on Bomarcs was negotiated with the United States by a Liberal government when the present Leader of the Opposition ... was our minister of external affairs.
Mr. Chairman, there was no negotiation of such an agreement by the previous government. I doubt if there was even at that time such a thing as the Bomarc B, which is the weapon we now have. It was under development at that time. So far as the position of the Social Credit party is concerned, the leader of that party made a strong plea for leadership, direction and decisiveness and said that all parties should at least take a stand on this matter so that people would know where they stood. He was complaining that we on this side were not definite. But the hon. member did not do very much in his statement last night, or in his broadcast the night before, or in the other statements which have appeared in the press in the last week or two, to clear up the ambiguities in the position taken by his own party on this important matter.
He is reported as having said on January 14 in Hong Kong that there is no need for nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. Nevertheless, he is reported as having said in Vancouver on January 16:
If acquisition of nuclear warheads by Canadian forces abroad means co-operation with NATO, then Canada should co-operate.
He is also reported as having said about the same time in Alberta that Americans should be permitted to make Canada their nuclear arsenal in case of war but that Canadian forces should not have such weapons. He said:
Nuclear weapons should be available to be brought to Canada in the event of a nuclear war and if that happened Canada should become the "arsenal" of the United States.
Meanwhile Social Credit does not favour extending the "nuclear club" but the party does think Canada should keep her NATO commitments even if it means equipping Canadian forces overseas with nuclear power.
I mention these things because we were reproved last night by the hon. gentleman for not being very decisive and clearcut in our statements. I must admit that the coleader of that party has been clearcut in his statement as reported in Le Devoir. He stated categorically that he opposes Canadian acquisition or use of nuclear weapons in any circumstances. Then, according to the reports, he went on to say that Canada should be like Ireland and Switzerland.
